claims.text: Nearly equiatomic five-transition-metal HENA are intrinsically structurally unstable above 0.5 Tm.
Elevated-temperature exposure causes chemical short-range-order clusters to form in these nanoparticles.
SRO clusters act as nucleation sites for phase separation.
SRO-driven phase separation causes breakdown of the initial single-phase solid solution.
HENA have lower thermal stability than their bulk counterparts.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of nanoparticles accelerates atomic diffusion.
SRO develops into large or percolating networks of ordered B2 or L21 phases.
Negative enthalpy of mixing between selected atomic pairs drives local chemical ordering.
High configurational entropy suppresses phase separation in bulk high-entropy alloys.
Reduced atomic coordination and high surface energy in nanoparticles lower the activation barrier for SRO formation.
Negative SRO parameters indicate attractive interactions between particular atomic pairs, including Cr-Hf or Al-Ni.
High nanoparticle diffusivity accelerates the conversion of ordered clusters into intermetallic precipitates.
The nanoparticle order-disorder transition temperature is lower than the corresponding bulk value.
Annealing will lead to nucleation and growth of secondary B2, sigma, or L21 phases.
New phase boundaries will cause a significant decrease in thermal conductivity.
Traditional random-solid-solution and bulk HEA models predict high thermal stability because of configurational entropy.
Traditional bulk HEA concepts predict sluggish diffusion and resistance to phase separation.
Particles larger than 100 nm become bulk-like because bulk configurational entropy dominates.
Systems in which all atomic pairs have positive enthalpies of mixing lack a driving force for SRO.
Below the ODTT, the random alloy state is thermodynamically stable.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that the random state is stable below the ODTT, while the mechanism invokes low-temperature attractive SRO and the cited ODTT evidence describes SRO or precipitation below the transition and homogenization as the ODTT is approached. The temperature direction assigned to ordering is therefore inconsistent with the theoretical constraint being invoked.
